clue.text: Standard applied to first US election, of which there are three

indicators.note: one piece is stuck onto the other, so the flag word follows the election word

parts.note: a primary is the preliminary vote in which a US party picks its candidate
a regiment's standard is its flag, also called its colours

explanation.surface: Reads like a political commentator noting a flag rule for an early US election, with an odd tally of three.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a relative clause: red, yellow and blue, the classic painter's trio, are what there are three of.
explanation.definitionFit: Painters' theory names exactly three base hues, red, yellow and blue, from which others are mixed.

clue.text: Ordinary folk are reaching the top, something MPs must get used to?

definitions.text: something MPs must get used to?

parts.note: the public are the general population
the contracted verb, as in the public's, written as an S
peaking means attaining a summit

explanation.surface: Common people rising to the top, which politicians must accept.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of Parliament must address the Commons and voters, so oratory is part of the job.

clue.text: Cross try line, giving no reaction

indicators.note: crossed wires are muddled, so these letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A rugby player scores a try without any response from the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like a verb about crossing the line; it is an anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Chemically inert substances do not react, so behaving that way means showing no response.

clue.text: Lose knack winding short bit of hose

indicators.note: twisting and turning, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A gardener losing the art of coiling a short garden hose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hose' suggests a garden pipe; it is hosiery.
explanation.definitionFit: Hose means stockings and socks, and a sock reaching only the ankle is a short piece of it.

clue.text: Lad collaring member for IOW town

indicators.note: seizing by the collar, so the young man holds the limb inside

parts.note: a youth is a young man
an arm is a limb, a member of the body

explanation.surface: A boy grabbing someone, a scene set in an island town.
explanation.walkthrough: IOW is the Isle of Wight, an island off England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: This port town lies on the north-west coast of the Isle of Wight.

clue.text: Utensil for cook with less guile?

definitions.meaning: a kitchen tool such as a tin or bottle device

explanation.surface: A kitchen gadget suited to a cook less cunning than most.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitchen tin device unseals containers, and someone more forthright is comparatively candid.

clue.text: Brief biography covering the start of Russian Revolution

indicators.note: the life story wraps around the single letter

parts.note: an obit, short for obituary, is a brief life story

indicators.note: only the opening letter is taken

explanation.surface: A short life story touching on the beginning of the 1917 revolution in Russia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolution' suggests 1917; it means one turn around a body.
explanation.definitionFit: A single circuit of a planet around its star is one revolution along its path.

clue.text: Answers used by chemists?

definitions.meaning: glass vessels with long necks, used for distilling

explanation.surface: Solutions that chemists supply.
explanation.definitionFit: Quick witty replies and long-necked distilling flasks share one word.

clue.text: What Blue Peter presenter is presumably doing patriotically?

definitions.text: What Blue Peter presenter is presumably doing patriotically?

parts.words: What Blue Peter presenter is presumably doing patriotically?
parts.note: Blue Peter is a long-running BBC children's programme, but a blue peter is also a signal flag, so whoever presents one is displaying a flag

explanation.walkthrough: Blue Peter is a British TV show for children; the blue peter is a naval flag signalling a ship is about to sail.
explanation.definitionFit: Displaying patriotism or national presence, literally or figuratively, is described by this idiom.

clue.text: Escape in one piece?

definitions.meaning: whimsically, something with no break in it, intact

explanation.surface: A prisoner hoping to get away without injury.
explanation.definitionFit: To escape is to get loose from restraint; read literally, the phrase describes something without any fracture.

clue.text: Particular delivery, necessity for cricket, voided catch

parts.note: you cannot play cricket without a bat

indicators.note: emptied of its contents, so only the outside letters of catch remain

explanation.surface: Cricket talk: a certain ball bowled, the equipment needed, and a dropped catch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivery' suggests a cricket ball bowled, fitting the surface; it is a consignment of goods.
explanation.definitionFit: A batch is one consignment or lot of goods sent or produced together.

clue.text: Fibre for carpet tiles recycled

indicators.note: used again in a new form, so these letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: Carpet tiles made from reused material, an eco-friendly flooring note.
explanation.definitionFit: Istle is a plant fibre from agave and yucca, used for cords, brushes and carpets.

clue.text: Best or worst contribution to innings?

definitions.meaning: to beat or topple, as in defeating a ruler
in cricket, a wild throw past the stumps gives the batting side extra runs, a fielder's worst contribution

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator asking which addition to a team's batting was the finest or the poorest.
explanation.definitionFit: To best a regime is to topple it; in cricket an errant return gifting runs carries the same name.

clue.text: Fox repelled by digging into waste matter

indicators.note: driven back, so the whole combination is read backwards
the little word burrows inside the waste word

parts.note: stools are faeces, bodily waste

explanation.surface: A fox driven off as it noses into rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fox' looks like an animal; it is a crafty person.
explanation.definitionFit: A fox is a cunning schemer, and a slyboots is likewise a crafty, artful person.

clue.text: Manages boards

definitions.meaning: climbs aboard a bus or train

explanation.surface: Reads like a line from a company report about who runs the directors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boards' suggests company directors; it is the verb of getting on a vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: Coping or progressing and stepping onto transport both use this phrasal verb.

clue.text: Deck me up rather like a Brontë sister?

indicators.note: in a down answer, up means read from bottom to top

parts.note: the Brontë sisters wrote as Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell, and the suffix -ish means somewhat like

explanation.surface: Someone asking to be dressed up like a Victorian novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deck' is the verb to adorn, not a ship's floor.
explanation.definitionFit: To deck something is to adorn or decorate it, adding ornament.

clue.text: Tough side on field for start of match

parts.note: a bully is a thug or tough
off is one side of a cricket field, opposite the leg side

explanation.surface: A hard-nosed team taking the pitch as the game begins.
explanation.definitionFit: In field hockey, play was traditionally begun with two players clashing sticks over the ball.

clue.text: Recurrent award shows approval of eco-friendly publishing

indicators.note: running back, so the honour's letters are read backwards

parts.note: an OBE is a British honour, Officer of the Order of the British Empire
OKs means approves or gives the nod

explanation.surface: A prize given year after year signals backing for green publishing.
explanation.definitionFit: Digital books need no paper, so publishing them is presented as kind to the environment.

clue.text: Former England 5 comes in promptly

indicators.note: the letter enters the punctuality phrase

parts.note: on time means punctually

indicators.note: 5-down's answer is a word for an opener, so the opening letter of England is meant

explanation.surface: An ex-England batsman arrives punctually.
explanation.walkthrough: '5' points to 5-down: England's opener is its first letter E.
explanation.definitionFit: Something one-time used to be so, just as a former holder once held a post.

clue.text: Flyer rejected assignment in space during project

indicators.note: the reversed group sits within the projecting word

parts.note: to jut is to stick out

indicators.note: sent back, so the combined letters run backwards
the task goes inside the space

parts.note: an em is a printer's space
a job is a task given

explanation.surface: A dismissed task in a space programme, perhaps a cancelled mission.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Space' suggests outer space but is a printer's unit; 'rejected' turns the job-in-space group backwards, giving MBOJE before it goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A flyer is anything that flies, and a large wide-bodied airliner is one example.

clue.text: Son's left recently to settle WWI conflict

indicators.note: gone away, so the son's letter is dropped

parts.note: just means a moment ago
S is the standard abbreviation for son
to land is to come to rest

explanation.surface: A son has just gone off to resolve a First World War dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Son's left' reads as 'the son has departed', removing S.
explanation.definitionFit: This 1916 North Sea naval battle between Britain and Germany was the war's largest sea clash.

clue.text: It's said parasitic insect will irritate the skin

indicators.note: spoken, so what follows is a sound-alike

parts.note: a tick is a blood-sucking parasite, and tick will contracts to tick'll

explanation.surface: A warning that a bug will make your skin itch.
explanation.walkthrough: Strictly a tick is an arachnid rather than an insect, but crosswords allow it.
explanation.definitionFit: To lightly stroke or tease the skin causes a twitching itch.

clue.text: Order to freeze work on fortifications

indicators.note: in an across answer, one piece placed on another follows it

parts.note: keeps are the strongholds of castles
to till is to work the soil

explanation.surface: A command to halt building work on castle defences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Freeze' is a command not to move, not about cold.
explanation.definitionFit: Telling someone to freeze is commanding them to stay motionless.

clue.text: Lady's laid up? This should get her going

indicators.note: in a down answer, set upwards, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: Anne's, Anne standing for any woman's name

explanation.surface: A woman confined to bed with illness needs a remedy to get moving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laid up' hints at illness as well as reversal; 'going' means bowel movement.
explanation.definitionFit: Senna is a herbal laxative, taken to relieve constipation.

clue.text: Hot drink, second of two almost finished

indicators.note: nearly complete, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: the latter is the second of two things mentioned

explanation.surface: Someone has nearly drained the second of two coffees.
explanation.definitionFit: A milky espresso coffee, served warm, is a familiar hot drink.

clue.text: Port on the Moray Firth making appearance in news

indicators.note: the look word sits inside the pair of new letters

parts.note: read as new plus new, each abbreviated N
an air is a look or manner

explanation.surface: A Scottish harbour town turning up in the headlines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'News' is read as two lots of 'new', each N; the Moray Firth is an inlet in north-east Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: This small Highland town lies on the Moray Firth coast and has a harbour.

clue.text: Wise guy currently packing gear for both sides

indicators.note: the gear holds the time word inside it

parts.note: kit is equipment
now means at present
as in a score of two-all, level for each team

explanation.surface: A smart-aleck currently loading equipment for both teams.
explanation.definitionFit: A wise guy is a smart-aleck who claims to have every answer.

clue.text: Barking 'woof', eg, breathed apt warning

indicators.note: barking means mad, so the letters go wild

explanation.surface: A dog's breathy woof is exactly the cue to keep clear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barking' looks like the dog's noise; it is British slang for crazy, the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A sign on a gate cautioning visitors about a guard animal is the fitting alert after a woof.
